docs.title: Testing
docs.text: The project uses a tiered testing strategy to ensure stability across multiple cloud and local providers:

docs.title: Testing Structure
docs.text:
• tests/unit: Unit Tests. High-isolation tests that use mocks to verify internal logic and CLI behavior without requiring external infrastructure.
  • tests/integration: Integration Tests. End-to-end tests that perform real operations against actual cloud infrastructure.
  • tests/compliance: Compliance Suite. Ensures every provider implements a consistent interface and meets the minimum functional baseline. Includes "Scenario Tests" for end-to-end user flows.

docs.title: Running Smoke Tests
docs.text:
Smoke tests are quick, high-level checks to verify that the CLI and providers load and execute basic commands without crashing.

# Run all smoke tests
PYTHONPATH=. pytest tests/smoke

docs.title: Configuration Validation Smoke Test
docs.text:
The tests/smoke/test_config.py smoke test validates the presence and correctness of both Cloudmesh and OpenStack configuration files (~/.config/cloudmesh/clouds.yaml and ~/.config/openstack/clouds.yaml). It checks that the YAML files are parsable and that required provider sections contain the necessary keys.

Run this test individually with:

PYTHONPATH=. pytest tests/smoke/test_config.py

It is also included when running the full smoke suite (pytest tests/smoke).

docs.title: Benchmark Results
docs.text:
Smoke tests automatically capture performance benchmarks (timers) and system information. These results are stored in a centralized repository for tracking improvements across different environments and users.

Requirements: To save results, you must have the results repository cloned locally at the project root's sibling directory: 

git clone git@github.com:cloudmesh/cloudmesh-ai-vm-results.git ..

Storage Path: Results are saved as .txt and .json files in the following structure: ../cloudmesh-ai-vm-results/<username>/smoke/

The username is retrieved from your ~/.config/cloudmesh/clouds.yaml configuration file.

Tests can be run in two modes:

  • Unit Mode (Default): Uses a standardized MockDriver to verify return types and basic logic without needing cloud credentials, ensuring a reliable functional baseline across all providers. 

    PYTHONPATH=. pytest -s tests/compliance/test_compliance.py

  • Integration Mode: Performs real operations against actual cloud infrastructure. Requires valid credentials in your configuration. 

    PYTHONPATH=. COMPLIANCE_MODE=integration pytest -s tests/compliance/test_compliance.py

The compliance suite also includes Scenario Tests (such as the "Zero-to-Hero" flow) to validate that the end-to-end user experience—from configuration validation to VM deletion—is consistent across all supported cloud and local providers.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
cmx vm purge is a high‑level clean‑up command that deletes all virtual machines, releases all floating IPs, and removes all reservations for a given cloud (or for every enabled cloud when no cloud is specified). This is intended for quickly resetting a cloud after a test run, teaching session, or any situation where a fresh environment is needed.

The command prompts for confirmation to avoid accidental data loss. For automated scripts the prompt can be bypassed using --yes (or -y).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
cmx vm purge [--cloud=CLOUD] [--yes | -y]
  • --cloud TEXT – Target a specific enabled cloud. If omitted, all enabled clouds are purged.
  • --yes, -y – Skip the interactive confirmation prompt (useful for CI/CD pipelines).

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
1. Safety Prompt – Unless --yes/-y is supplied, the command asks: 
    Are you sure you want to purge all resources for cloud <cloud_name>? [y/N]:
  2. VM Deletion – Iterates over each VM returned by the provider and calls provider.delete(name).
  3. Floating IP Release – If the provider implements list_floating_ips() and release_floating_ip_by_ip(address), those are used. Otherwise it falls back to the existing release_floating_ip(name).
  4. Reservation Removal – If the provider implements list_reservations() and delete_reservation(res_id), those are called (e.g., Chameleon uses chi.lease.delete_lease).
  5. Logging – Each action is logged via the shared console object. Errors are reported but the command continues processing remaining items.
  6. Idempotence – Running the command again after a successful purge results in “nothing to delete” messages rather than errors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
cmx vm purge                     # Interactive prompt, all clouds
cmx vm purge --cloud chameleon   # Interactive, only Chameleon
cmx vm purge -y                  # Non‑interactive, all clouds
cmx vm purge --cloud multipass -y

docs.title: Testing (recommended)
docs.text:
Unit tests should mock the provider APIs to verify:

  • The confirmation prompt is displayed and can be bypassed with --yes.
  • delete, release_floating_ip_by_ip, and delete_reservation are called for each resource.
  • Errors are logged but do not abort the purge.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The cmx vm status command provides a concise audit of the resources currently allocated in a cloud provider (or across all enabled clouds). It lists:

  1. Running VMs – name, status, IP address, image, flavor, etc.
  2. Floating IPs – address, attached VM (if any), and status.
  3. Reservations / Leases – reservation ID, type, status, start time, and end time.

The output is a human‑readable table divided into the three sections above. An optional --json flag produces the same information as a JSON document, suitable for scripting.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
cmx vm status [--cloud=CLOUD] [--json]
  • --cloud TEXT – Limit the audit to a specific enabled cloud. If omitted, all enabled clouds are included.
  • --json – Emit the information as a JSON document instead of a table.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
cmx vm status                     # All clouds, human‑readable table
cmx vm status --cloud openstack   # Only OpenStack cloud
cmx vm status --json              # JSON output for all clouds

docs.title: JSON Format
docs.text:
When --json is used, the output is structured per cloud:

{
  "cloud": "openstack",
  "vms": [
    {"name": "my-vm", "status": "ACTIVE", "ip": "203.0.113.5", "image": "ubuntu-20.04", "flavor": "m1.small"}
  ],
  "floating_ips": [
    {"address": "203.0.113.5", "attached": "my-vm", "status": "ACTIVE"}
  ],
  "reservations": [
    {"id": "lease-123", "type": "node_reservations", "status": "ACTIVE", "start": "2026-10-01T12:00:00", "end": "2026-10-08T12:00:00"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Behaviour notes
docs.text:
• Providers that do not support floating IPs or reservations will show empty lists for those sections.
  • Errors retrieving data for a particular cloud are reported, but the command continues processing other clouds.

docs.title: Multipass Provider
docs.text: The Multipass provider allows you to manage lightweight Ubuntu virtual machines on your local machine. It leverages the Canonical Multipass daemon to handle VM orchestration, providing a fast and consistent development environment.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Multipass is used to create and manage local VMs. Unlike traditional virtualization, Multipass is designed for rapid deployment of Ubuntu instances, making it ideal for testing cloud-like environments locally.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The Multipass provider uses the following configuration settings in clouds.yaml:

Setting Description Default image The Ubuntu image version to use for launches. 22.04 cpus Number of CPU cores assigned to each VM. Host default memory Amount of RAM assigned to each VM (e.g., 2GiB). Host default disk Disk size assigned to each VM (e.g., 10GiB). Host default

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
clouds:
  multipass:
    image: "24.04"
    cpus: 2
    memory: "4GiB"
    disk: "20GiB"

docs.title: VM Lifecycle
docs.text:
• cmx vm start [NAME]: Launches a new VM. If no name is provided, one is automatically generated using the {username}-{counter} pattern.
  • cmx vm stop [NAME]: Stops a running VM.
  • cmx vm restart [NAME]: Stops and then starts a VM.
  • cmx vm delete [NAME]: Deletes a VM and purges its data from the system.

docs.title: Resource Discovery
docs.text:
• cmx vm list: Displays all local Multipass VMs, including their status and IP addresses.
  • cmx vm info [NAME]: Shows detailed internal metadata for a specific VM.
  • cmx vm image: Lists available Ubuntu images that can be used for launches.

docs.title: VM Interaction
docs.text:
• cmx vm run [NAME] [COMMAND]: Executes a command inside the VM via the Multipass agent.
  • cmx vm login [NAME]: Provides the SSH connection string to access the VM.
  • cmx vm upload-key [PATH] --name [NAME]: Uploads a public SSH key to the VM for passwordless access.

docs.title: Local Environment Portability
docs.text: The Multipass provider is designed to be portable across different Windows shells. It automatically detects whether it should use multipass.exe or multipass based on the environment (CMD, PowerShell, or Git Bash), ensuring consistent behavior regardless of how the CLI is invoked.

docs.title: Daemon Management
docs.text: On macOS, you can reset the Multipass daemon if it becomes unresponsive using: cmx vm reset This performs a kickstart of the com.canonical.multipassd system service. 48 | 49 | ### Snapshot Management 50 | 51 | - cmx vm snapshot <NAME> <SNAPSHOT>: Creates a snapshot of the specified VM using multipass snapshot. 52 | - cmx vm list-snapshots <NAME>: Lists all snapshots for a VM. Internally this calls multipass snapshots or extracts the snapshot list from multipass info --format json. 53 | - cmx vm restore <NAME> <SNAPSHOT>: Restores a VM to the state captured in the named snapshot via multipass restore. 54 | `

docs.text:

docs.title: OpenStack Provider
docs.text: OpenStack is a powerful open-source cloud computing platform that provides a unified interface for managing large-scale pools of compute, storage, and networking resources. This provider allows cloudmesh-ai-vm to interact with any OpenStack-compliant cloud, including private clouds and specialized research clouds like Chameleon and Jetstream.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The OpenStack provider typically relies on a standard OpenStack clouds.yaml file located at ~/.config/openstack/clouds.yaml.

To define a cloud in clouds.yaml:

clouds:
  my-openstack-cloud:
    auth:
      auth_url: https://openstack.example.com:5000/v3
      username: "my-user"
      password: "my-password"
      project_domain_id: "default"
      project_id: "my-project-id"
    region_name: "RegionOne"
    interface: "public"

You can then set this as your default in the cloudmesh configuration:

openstack:
  default_cloud: my-openstack-cloud
  image: ubuntu-22.04
  flavor: m1.small

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Scaling: Easily manage dozens of VMs across different regions.
  • Advanced Lifecycle: Support for shelving (saving VM state and freeing resources) and unshelving.
  • Network Control: Comprehensive management of Security Groups and firewall rules.
  • Hardware Profiles: Use Flavors to specify exact CPU, RAM, and disk requirements.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Set OpenStack as the active provider
cmx vm provider set openstack

# List available flavors in the cloud
cmx vm flavor

# Start a VM using a specific flavor
cmx vm start my-os-vm --flavor m1.medium

# Shelve a VM to free up resources
cmx vm shelve my-os-vm

docs.title: OpenStack Security and SSH
docs.text: This guide describes SSH key management, security groups, and VM access for OpenStack-based providers such as Chameleon Cloud and Jetstream.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The OpenStack provider requires the OpenStack CLI to be installed and configured. The active cloud configuration should also include the SSH private key and default VM user when SSH access is required.

Example configuration:

key_path: ~/.ssh/id_rsa
user: ubuntu
security_group: default

Note: The exact image, username, credentials, and security-group requirements may differ between OpenStack deployments.

docs.title: List Keys
docs.text:
List SSH keys available in the active provider:

cmx key list

docs.title: Upload a Public Key
docs.text:
Upload an existing public SSH key:

cmx key upload ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub

If no path is supplied, the command resolves the key path in the following priority: 1. key_path defined in clouds.yaml for the active provider. 2. Local file ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub. 3. Local file ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub. 4. Any single file matching ~/.ssh/*.pub. (If multiple files match, an error is raised and manual configuration in clouds.yaml is required).

A custom cloud key name can also be specified:

cmx key upload ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub --name my-cloud-key

Note: If --name is omitted, the tool first checks for key_name in clouds.yaml. If still missing, the provider derives the key name from the public-key filename.

docs.title: Delete a Key
docs.text:
Delete a key from the active provider:

cmx key delete my-cloud-key

Important: Deleting the cloud copy of a public key does not delete your local private key.

docs.title: Security Groups
docs.text: Security groups control network access to OpenStack VMs.

docs.title: List Security Groups
docs.text: cmx vm security-group list

docs.title: Inspect a Security Group
docs.text: cmx vm security-group info default

docs.title: Create a Security Group
docs.text:
Create a group for SSH access:

cmx vm security-group create ssh-access \
    --description "Allow SSH access"

docs.title: Add an SSH Rule
docs.text:
Allow inbound TCP port 22 from a trusted network:

cmx vm security-group rule add ssh-access \
    --protocol tcp \
    --port 22 \
    --cidr 192.0.2.0/24 \
    --direction ingress

Security Tip: Replace 192.0.2.0/24 with the specific network that should be allowed to connect. Avoid using 0.0.0.0/0 for SSH unless public SSH access is intentionally required. Restricting the CIDR reduces unnecessary exposure of port 22.

docs.title: List Rules
docs.text: cmx vm security-group rule list ssh-access

docs.title: Associate the Group with a VM
docs.text: cmx vm security-group add my-vm ssh-access

docs.title: Remove the Group from a VM
docs.text: cmx vm security-group remove my-vm ssh-access

docs.title: Remove a Rule
docs.text:
First, obtain the rule ID:

cmx vm security-group rule list ssh-access

Then remove it:

cmx vm security-group rule remove ssh-access <rule-id>

docs.title: Delete the Security Group
docs.text:
cmx vm security-group delete ssh-access

Note: Remove the group from all associated VMs before attempting to delete it if required by your OpenStack deployment.

docs.title: Connecting to a VM
docs.text:
Once the VM has network connectivity, an appropriate security group, and the correct SSH key, inspect its connection information:

cmx vm login my-vm

Start an interactive SSH session:

cmx vm ssh my-vm

Generate SSH configuration information:

cmx vm ssh-config my-vm

Run a command remotely:

cmx vm run my-vm "hostname"

The OpenStack implementation uses the configured key_path and user values when establishing SSH-based connections.

docs.title: Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
A typical secure setup follows these steps:

  1. Create or select an SSH key pair locally.
  2. Upload only the public key to OpenStack.
  3. Create a dedicated security group.
  4. Allow SSH only from the required source CIDR.
  5. Associate the security group with the VM.
  6. Verify the VM connection information.
  7. Connect using cmx vm ssh or execute commands with cmx vm run.

Example execution:

# Upload public key
cmx key upload ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub --name research-key

# Create security group
cmx vm security-group create research-ssh \
    --description "SSH access for research VM"

# Add inbound SSH rule for trusted CIDR
cmx vm security-group rule add research-ssh \
    --protocol tcp \
    --port 22 \
    --cidr 192.0.2.0/24 \
    --direction ingress

# Attach security group to instance
cmx vm security-group add research-vm research-ssh

# Inspect login info and connect
cmx vm login research-vm
cmx vm ssh research-vm

docs.title: Provider Support
docs.text:
The commands in this guide describe functionality implemented by the OpenStack provider. Chameleon Cloud and Jetstream use the OpenStack provider path, but authentication, images, network configuration, quotas, and site-specific policies may differ.

Other providers may implement only a subset of these operations. For example, a provider may support listing security groups without supporting creation or rule management. Unsupported operations should be handled through the provider feature interface rather than assumed to be available on every cloud.
